lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about how honeybees communicate. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I'm going to look at one of the most remarkable communication systems in the animal world: the way honeybees share information.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: Let's start with some background. A healthy colony in summer can contain tens of thousands of bees. Nearly all of them are female workers, living with a single queen and, at certain times of year, some hundreds of males, which are known as drones.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: A worker's job changes as she gets older. Young workers stay inside the hive, cleaning cells and feeding the larvae. Then, at around three weeks old, they become foragers and start flying out to collect food.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: Foragers bring back nectar, which the colony turns into honey, and they also gather pollen. Pollen is the main source of protein for the young bees, so a colony simply can't grow without it.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: On hot days they carry water back as well, which is used to cool the hive.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: Now, one forager on her own can only visit so many flowers. The real strength of a colony is that a bee who finds a good source of food can tell her sisters exactly where it is.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: She does this with what's called the waggle dance. Its meaning was first worked out by the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who shared a Nobel Prize in 1973 for his work on animal behaviour.
lines.say: She does this with what's called the waggle dance. Its meaning was first worked out by the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who shared a Nobel Prize in nineteen seventy-three for his work on animal behaviour.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: You might expect a dance to be performed outside, at the entrance to the hive, where there's light and space. In fact, it happens inside, on the vertical surface of the comb, in complete darkness.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: So how do the other bees follow it? They can't see the dancer, so they crowd around her and keep in contact by touch, using their antennae to follow her movements.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: The dance has two parts. The bee runs in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, and that's the waggle run. Then she circles back to the start and does it again, over and over.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: The direction of the waggle run is the clever part. If the bee runs straight up the comb, it means 'fly towards the sun'.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: If she runs at an angle of, say, forty degrees to the right of vertical, the food is forty degrees to the right of the sun. So the angle on the comb matches the angle outside.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: Distance is shown in a different way: by the duration of the waggle run, in other words, how long it lasts. The longer the waggle, the further away the food.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: And a bee that has found a really rich patch of flowers dances with more energy, and repeats the dance many more times than one that has found only a few. So the number of repeats tells the others about the quality of the food, not just where it is.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: For food that's very close to the hive, the dance is much simpler. The bee just runs round in small circles, and this has traditionally been called the round dance.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: The dance isn't the only clue, though. The dancer also carries the scent of the flowers on her body, and the followers pick it up.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: So when they arrive in the right area, they know which flowers to look for. They may be offered a taste of the nectar too, but the scent is the key clue.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: Bees also communicate with chemicals called pheromones. One of the best known is the alarm signal. When a guard bee at the entrance senses danger, she releases a chemical that tells other bees to come and defend the hive.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: Beekeepers will tell you that this alarm pheromone smells rather like bananas. So it's not a good idea to eat one just before you open a hive!

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: Perhaps the most impressive example of bee communication happens when a colony swarms. In spring, the old queen leaves with a large part of the workforce, and they gather in a cluster, often on the branch of a tree, while they look for a new home.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: A few hundred scout bees fly off and inspect possible sites, such as hollow trees. When a scout finds a good one, she comes back and dances for it.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: Other scouts go and check her site, and if they like it, they dance for it too. Gradually, the best site attracts more and more supporters, until enough scouts are gathered there at the same time. Then the whole swarm flies off to its new home.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: It isn't a fight between the scouts, and no single bee is in charge. Scientists who study swarms have often compared the process to a vote, and it usually leads the bees to the best site available.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: Finally, a word about threats. Honeybees face many problems, including disease and the loss of the wild flowers they feed on.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: But one threat affects their ability to communicate quite directly. Research suggests that some pesticides can make it harder for foragers to find their way back to the hive, and of course a bee that can't get home can't share what she has found.

lines.speaker: LECTURER
lines.text: Next week, we'll see how ants use chemical trails to solve a very similar problem.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: That is the end of Part 4.

pairs: the main source of protein for the young bees
31.why: Foragers bring back nectar and also gather pollen. Pollen gives protein to young bees, which matches the end of the note.
31.trap: Honey is mentioned, but bees make honey from nectar; they do not collect it. Water is also collected, but it is used for cooling, not protein.

evidence.quote: on the vertical surface of the comb

32.why: The dance happens inside the hive, on the vertical surface of the comb.
32.trap: The entrance to the hive is mentioned first, but the lecturer says 'In fact, it happens inside'.

33.why: The bees can't see in the dark hive, so they follow the dancer by touch, using their antennae.
33.trap: 'Antennae' is how they touch, but the note needs the word after 'by'.
